lesson.title: Just Two Levels: How Digital Signals Represent Data
lesson.summary: A digital signal uses only a small, fixed set of values, usually two, to represent bits, and that restriction is exactly what makes it possible to regenerate a perfectly clean copy even after long distances.
lesson.body:
A digital signal is a signal restricted to a small, finite number of distinct values, most commonly just two, representing the binary digits 0 and 1 that make up a bit, the basic unit of digital information. Instead of the smooth, continuously varying signal covered in the previous chapter, a digital signal jumps between a small set of fixed levels, for example a low voltage representing a 0 bit and a higher voltage representing a 1 bit.

This restriction is exactly what gives digital signals their key advantage. A receiver does not need to measure a digital signal's exact value, only decide which of the small set of allowed levels it is closest to. If a 0 bit is sent as roughly 0 volts and a 1 bit as roughly 5 volts, a receiver reading 4.6 volts due to some noise on the line can still correctly conclude a 1 was sent, because 4.6 is much closer to 5 than to 0. Small amounts of noise simply do not change the outcome, as long as the noise is not large enough to push the reading past the decision threshold between levels. Not every digital signal is limited to just two levels either: some systems use four, eight, or more distinct levels so that a single change in the signal can represent more than one bit at a time, an idea that comes up again in the chapter on modulation.

As an example, suppose a link transmits at 10 Mbps and needs to send the byte 01001101. At 10 Mbps, each bit occupies 1 divided by 10,000,000 seconds, which is 100 nanoseconds. The full 8 bit byte, sent as a sequence of 8 discrete voltage levels one after another, therefore occupies 8 times 100 nanoseconds, or 800 nanoseconds, on the link.

This noise tolerance leads to a second, arguably even more important advantage over analog signals. Because a digital receiver only needs to decide which of a few levels was sent, a device partway along a long path can regenerate the signal rather than merely amplify it: it detects which bit was intended and outputs a brand new, perfectly clean pulse representing that exact bit, discarding any accumulated noise entirely. This is fundamentally different from an analog amplifier, which boosts noise right along with the signal, as discussed in the previous chapter. Regeneration is why long haul digital systems, from undersea fiber optic cables to cellular backbone networks, can carry data across enormous distances with many repeaters in between and still deliver an essentially exact copy of the original bits.

The specific rules for mapping bits to voltage or light levels over time are called line coding schemes, with names like NRZ and Manchester encoding describing different ways to handle timing and to avoid long runs of identical bits that could make it hard for a receiver to stay synchronized. The next chapter builds on both digital and analog signals to cover modulation, the technique of using digital data, or an analog signal like voice, to systematically vary an underlying carrier signal so it can travel effectively over a particular medium.
